title: Graph-theoretic framework for semi-Markov networks: transient and stationary occupation probabilities, hitting times and weak ergodicity breaking
abstract: Semi-Markov networks provide a natural framework for describing stochastic transitions between coarse-grained states with non-exponential dwell times, with applications ranging from biophysics and neuroscience to epidemiology and finance. Here, it is shown that finite semi-Markov networks admit explicit combinatorial representations of their Laplace-transformed occupation probabilities and hitting-time distributions as sums over weighted spanning trees and forests of an augmented graph. These representations yield asymptotic results, including a generalization of the Markov Chain Tree Theorem to semi-Markov networks, in which the rate constants replaced by pseudo-rates given by the inverse mean sojourn time weighted by the exit probability through this channel, as well as the long-time scaling of hitting-time survival probabilities in the presence of infinite-mean sojourn times. They also extend recently derived combinatorial formulas for hitting-time moments to the semi-Markov setting. In particular, the mean hitting-time formula coincides with that of a Markov network with the corresponding pseudo-rates, which also yields a short proof of the constancy of Kemeny's constant for finite-mean semi-Markov networks. Finally, we use the same framework to show that weak ergodicity breaking occurs generically for time-additive state observables that are nonconstant on the support of the limiting distribution in heavy-tailed semi-Markov networks.
summary: This paper introduces a powerful graph-theoretic framework to analyze semi-Markov networks, which model systems with non-exponential waiting times. It extends combinatorial results, such as those involving spanning trees, to derive explicit formulas for occupation probabilities and hitting times. This work is significant for understanding complex stochastic dynamics, particularly in regimes exhibiting weak ergodicity breaking.
main_problem: To develop a rigorous graph-theoretic framework for analyzing semi-Markov networks, extending established results from standard Markov chains to systems with non-exponential dwell times.
main_result: The framework successfully generalizes combinatorial representations (like those involving spanning trees) to semi-Markov networks, providing formulas for occupation probabilities and hitting times, and characterizing weak ergodicity breaking in heavy-tailed regimes.
method: The analysis heavily relies on Laplace transforms, extending the Markov Chain Tree Theorem by replacing constant rates with memory kernels, and utilizing graph theory on an augmented graph to derive matrix inverses.
model_or_system: The model is a semi-Markov network defined on a finite directed graph, characterized by non-exponential sojourn time distributions, which allows for complex stochastic transitions between coarse-grained states.
key_observables: Occupation probabilities (transient and stationary), hitting-time distributions and moments, and the characterization of weak ergodicity breaking via time-additive state observables.
important_parameters: The analysis distinguishes between finite-mean and infinite-mean sojourn times, and uses pseudo-rates derived from the inverse mean sojourn time.
main_assumptions: The core extension assumes that the graph-theoretic structure generalizes naturally, unlike spectral methods, and the analysis often relies on Tauberian theorems for asymptotic limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph structure, the construction of an augmented graph G* for analysis, and the convergence of occupation probabilities for both finite-mean (Gamma) and heavy-tailed (Pareto type II) cases.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the semi-Markov process and its Laplace transforms, deriving the generalized master equation using graph theory on an augmented graph, and finally applying these tools to calculate stationary limits, hitting times, and analyze weak ergodicity breaking.
why_interesting: While the focus is on classical stochastic processes, the mathematical tools—especially the use of graph theory to solve complex linear systems derived from time-domain dynamics—are highly relevant to analyzing open quantum systems or quantum networks where non-Markovian dynamics are present.
